summary: Illustrates the growth of the Internet from 1981 to 1991 by examining entries in the Domain Name System and in the host tables used before DNS. It is a statistical look at how many hosts and networks appeared over that decade.

plainLanguage.summary: Like measuring a child against a door frame each year, this paper counts how many computers were on the Internet over ten years to show how fast it grew.

questions: how many hosts were on the early internet
how did researchers count internet hosts in the 1980s
subtitle: Measuring how the Internet grew from 213 hosts in 1981 to over 700,000 in 1992

tldr.problem: The Internet's size and growth rate were not well documented as it transitioned from pre-DNS host tables to the Domain Name System.
tldr.mechanism: A program called ZONE was written to walk the DNS tree and collect information about all registered hosts and domains, allowing statistics to be gathered about the network's expansion.
tldr.outcome: The data showed exponential growth: from 213 hosts in August 1981 to 727,000 hosts by January 1992, with the growth accelerating after 1988 when DNS problems were resolved.

today: RFC 1296 is an Informational RFC documenting the history of Internet growth in the early 1990s. This data is historical but remains the most comprehensive record of how quickly the Internet expanded during this critical period of expansion.

sections.title: Counting Internet Hosts Over a Decade
sections.content:
This RFC documents the growth of the Internet from 1981 through 1991 by examining how many hosts and domains existed at various points in time. For the early years before the Domain Name System (DNS) existed, data came from archived copies of the official host table maintained by the Network Information Center at SRI. After DNS was introduced around 1984, a program called ZONE was used to collect data by querying domain servers directly.

The study is valuable because it provides the first systematic record of Internet growth during its critical early years, showing how the network expanded from a small academic system to a much larger commercial and institutional infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper tracks how many computers were connected to the Internet by counting them in two ways: before DNS (by reading old record books) and after DNS (by asking domain servers). It shows the Internet grew really fast, especially after 1988.

sections.title: The ZONE Program: How Data Was Collected
sections.content:
The ZONE (Zealot Of Name Edification) program was written in 1986 to help sites transition from the old host table system to DNS. Instead of being used for that purpose, it became useful for collecting statistics. ZONE works by connecting to domain name servers and asking them to transfer their complete zone data using the standard DNS zone transfer mechanism (AXFR). When it receives a name server record (NS), it adds that domain to a list to process next. When it receives host records (A, CNAME, HINFO, MX), it stores the host information in memory.

Over time, ZONE became the primary tool for measuring Internet size. Initially it produced massive wall-size charts of the domain tree, but as domains grew, it was modified to collect only the essential information: host names and IP addresses. By 1992, ZONE was run every three months at SRI to produce updated statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: ZONE is like a robot that calls up every domain server and says: 'Please give me the complete list of computers in your domain.' It stores all that information and counts how many unique computers it found.

sections.title: Data Collection Limitations
sections.content:
The statistics collected by ZONE are not perfect. Some sites refuse to allow zone transfers of their domain servers, so those hosts are never counted. In the January 1, 1992 run, ZONE failed to retrieve data from about 800 out of 17,000 domains. Additionally, not all Internet hosts are registered in DNS; many sites keep local machines off the global registry. For these reasons, the ZONE numbers represent a minimum count of actual Internet hosts.

However, some over-counting also occurs. DNS data contains random misformatted entries, servers that claim authority for domains they do not actually manage, and hosts in domains that were renamed and left with old entries. Manual review suggests the over-counting is less significant than the under-counting, so ZONE data is considered a reasonable lower bound on the true Internet size.
sections.plainLanguage: ZONE can't see every computer: some sites hide theirs, and some mistakes in DNS make it look like there are more than there really are. But the hidden ones are more of a problem than the wrong ones, so the numbers are probably a bit too low.

sections.title: The Dramatic Growth
sections.content:
The data reveals explosive growth in Internet size. In August 1981, there were 213 hosts. By February 1986, that had grown to 2,308 hosts, representing a roughly five-fold increase over five years. Then growth accelerated dramatically. By November 1986, just nine months later, there were 5,089 hosts. One year later in December 1987, there were 28,174 hosts.

The most dramatic growth came after 1988, when ZONE could finally collect complete data due to fixes in the BIND DNS implementation. From 1988 onward, growth was nearly exponential: 33,000 hosts in July 1988, 80,000 in January 1989, 313,000 in October 1990, and finally 727,000 hosts by January 1992. The numbers roughly doubled every year for the final four years measured.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet stayed tiny for the first five years, then started growing faster. From 1988 onward, it doubled in size roughly every year. In just four years it went from 30,000 computers to 700,000.

sections.title: Distribution Patterns in the Data
sections.content:
Beyond total counts, the RFC breaks down how hosts and domains were distributed. Most domains were in the .edu domain (243,020 hosts as of January 1992), followed by .com (181,361), .gov (46,463), and national domains like .au (Australia, 31,622) and .de (Germany, 31,016). The .org and .net domains contained fewer hosts by this date. Growth rates varied by domain: military (.mil) grew 26% in just three months, while .net actually shrunk 49%, likely due to reorganizations.

The data also shows that most hosts had exactly one IP address (715,143 hosts), while a small fraction had multiple addresses for redundancy or load balancing. Common host names reveal the Unix tradition of naming computers after planets, mythological figures, and cartoon characters: Venus, Pluto, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn led the list, along with hundreds of hosts named Mac (with numbers), and other creative names like Hobbes, Gandalf, and Spock.
sections.plainLanguage: The breakdown shows which parts of the Internet grew fastest: colleges dominated, then companies, then government. Most computers had one name, and people liked naming them after planets and cartoon characters.
